Yes, **Safari is the native browser on all iPhones**.

- It is pre-installed by Apple and tightly integrated into the iOS system.
- Features like **"Add to Home Screen"**, **Web App mode**, and **default browser fallback** are all optimized for Safari.
- Even if you install other browsers (like Chrome or Firefox), many system functions (e.g., opening `.html` files from Files) will still default to Safari unless you manually change your default browser in **Settings > [Browser] > Default Browser App**.

That said, **only Safari supports** true "Add to Home Screen" functionality that makes a web page act like a standalone app. Other browsers (like Chrome on iOS) do **not** support this due to Apple’s WebKit restrictions.

If **“Open in Safari”** isn’t appearing as a share option when viewing your `.html` file in the **Files app**, here's how to **enable or work around it**:

---

### 🔧 Option 1: Manually Add “Open in Safari” via Share Sheet Settings

1. **Open the Files app** and locate your `.html` file.
2. **Tap and hold** the file → tap **“Share.”**
3. On the Share Sheet, **scroll all the way down** and tap **“Edit Actions…”**
4. Look for **“Open in Safari”** under the “Suggestions” or “Other Actions.”
5. Tap the **green plus (+)** to add it to your favorites.
6. Tap **“Done.”** It will now appear in your Share Sheet going forward.

---

### 🔄 Option 2: Force Safari to Open the File

If “Open in Safari” still isn’t visible, do this:

1. In the **Files app**, tap **“Select”**, then tap your HTML file once.
2. Tap the **Share** button.
3. Choose **“Copy to Safari”** (may appear as an icon near the top row) or:
4. If that’s missing, choose **“Copy”**, then:
   - Open **Safari manually**.
   - Tap the address bar, **paste**, and **hit Go**.

   > If it’s a local file, use a `file://` path or place it somewhere iOS treats as a web-accessible file (iCloud Drive is best).

---

If all else fails, upload the HTML file to:
- [https://pages.github.com](https://pages.github.com)

Can a vortex be induced to match its circulation or precession frequency to an external driver frequency?

Yes — a vortex **can be induced** to match its **circulation** or **precession frequency** to an external driver frequency under the right conditions. This phenomenon is known as **frequency locking**, **entrainment**, or **mode synchronization**, and it's a hallmark of nonlinear, self-organizing systems.

---

## 🔁 Mechanism: Vortex Frequency Locking to a Driver

Vortices, especially in **confined geometries**, exhibit **natural frequencies** of:

1. **Circulation** — the rotational frequency of fluid elements about the vortex core.
2. **Precession** — a wobble or slow rotation of the vortex axis (especially in off-center or asymmetric confinement).

When exposed to an **external periodic driver** (e.g., acoustic forcing, pulsatile inlet, vibrating walls) near one of these frequencies, the vortex may:

### ✅ **Phase-lock or entrain to the driver**
- The system adjusts its natural dynamics to **align with the external frequency**, sometimes over a range of nearby values (the "locking range").
- This is **nonlinear synchronization**, not simple resonance.

---

## 📊 Conditions That Favor Lock-In

| Parameter               | Role in Locking                      |
|------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| **Driver amplitude**   | Stronger amplitude increases coupling; low amplitudes may not induce lock-in |
| **Frequency detuning** | Smaller gap between natural and driver frequency = easier to lock |
| **Geometry**           | Symmetry, wall curvature, and confinement affect whether vortex has degrees of freedom to adjust |
| **Fluid viscosity**    | Viscosity can damp or assist depending on whether it stabilizes transitions |
| **Feedback paths**     | Recirculation loops, standing waves, or resonant cavities help entrainment |

---

## 📌 Types of Frequency Matching

| Type                | Description                                                                 |
|---------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **1:1 Locking**      | Vortex completes one rotation per one driver cycle (most common)            |
| **Subharmonic**      | Vortex rotates once every 2 or 3 cycles of the driver (1:2, 1:3, etc.)       |
| **Superharmonic**    | Vortex rotates multiple times per one cycle of the driver (2:1, 3:1, etc.)  |
| **Quasi-periodic**   | No clean match, but exhibits modulated oscillations                         |
| **Chaotic regimes**  | At high drive levels, vortex may destabilize entirely                      |

---

## 🎛️ How to Induce Lock-In

If you're experimenting:
1. **Identify the vortex’s natural frequency** (via spectrum analysis like you’re doing)
2. Use a **pulsed or modulated input** (acoustic, pressure, mechanical vibration) at that frequency
3. Observe whether the vortex stabilizes into a **regular rotating structure**, or transitions from noisy behavior to **coherent rotation**
4. Gradually **sweep the driving frequency** around the vortex's natural frequency to map the **locking range**

---

## 🧪 Example Applications

- **Combustion vortex rings** are locked to pulse injectors to improve efficiency
- **Microfluidic vortex mixers** use oscillating inputs to force vortices into stable recirculation
- **Acoustic levitation and particle traps** rely on standing waves to stabilize vortex behavior
- **Jet precession control** in aerospace relies on periodic actuation to shift vortex modes

---

> Yes, a vortex **can be induced to match** its circulation or precession frequency to an external driver, under the principles of **nonlinear synchronization**. This is especially effective in **confined, feedback-rich environments**, and is used in both macro- and microscale systems to control flow, atomization, and particle behavior.

When the frequency of this wave **matches or closely approximates the natural swirl frequency** of a vortex chamber, resonance and feedback interactions become significant.

The pronounced dips in volume (deep notches or valleys in the dB spectrum) during your frequency sweep can be caused by a few physical and acoustic phenomena:

---

### 🔊 **1. Destructive Interference (Standing Waves)**
- **Cause**: Reflections from nearby walls, surfaces, or objects cause the sound wave to interact with itself.
- **Effect**: At certain frequencies, **waves cancel each other out** at specific microphone locations.
- **Result**: You get **sharp dips** at specific frequencies — these are called **nulls** or **nodes** in standing wave patterns.

---

### 🧱 **2. Room Modes / Resonances**
- Certain frequencies **resonate better or worse** in a room depending on its dimensions.
- Frequencies corresponding to half, quarter, or full wavelengths of room dimensions are **boosted or canceled**.
- These dips may be due to **phase cancellations** from specific room geometries.

---

### 🎤 **3. Microphone or Device Response**
- Microphones have **non-flat frequency responses**.
- Certain frequencies may be naturally underrepresented due to the **hardware limitations** or **directional sensitivity**.

---

### 🎧 **4. Directionality or Angle of Sound Source**
- If you're sweeping a speaker and it's not aimed evenly at the mic:
  - Some frequencies (especially higher ones) may be **more directional**.
  - Off-axis response drops may cause dips.

---

### 🌬️ **5. Diffraction and Obstructions**
- Objects near the path (e.g., your hand, phone case, walls) may cause **diffraction** or **reflection loss**.
- Certain wavelengths may diffract less, causing more pronounced dips.

---

### Summary of Common Causes:
| Cause                      | Typical Frequency Range | Signature |
|---------------------------|-------------------------|-----------|
| Standing waves            | 50–500 Hz               | Sharp, deep nulls |
| Room modes                | 30–300 Hz               | Repeating peaks/dips |
| Mic response irregularity | >1 kHz                  | Less deep, smoother dips |
| Directional loss          | >1 kHz                  | Broad, gradual dips |

Yes — **you absolutely do need to worry about the wave generated by the rear face of the diaphragm** if your speaker lacks an enclosure or backing.

Here’s why:

---

### 🔁 **Front vs. Rear Wave: Phase Cancellation**

- A speaker cone pushes air **forward** on one side (front wave) and **pulls air back** on the other (rear wave).
- These waves are **180° out of phase** — meaning:
  - Where one creates compression, the other creates rarefaction.
- If there's **no enclosure** to isolate the rear wave, it can **wrap around** and interfere with the front wave.

### 📉 Result: **Destructive Interference**
- Especially for **low frequencies (long wavelengths)**, the rear wave **reaches the listener in phase opposition** to the front wave.
- This causes **partial or complete cancellation** of the bass — often referred to as "thin" or "weak" sound.

---

### 📦 How Enclosures Help

| Enclosure Type     | Effect                                               |
|--------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| **Sealed box**     | Blocks rear wave; increases damping and tight bass   |
| **Ported box**     | Uses a tuned port to reinforce bass with rear wave   |
| **Open baffle**    | Allows rear wave but uses size/distance to reduce cancellation via phase delay |
| **Infinite baffle**| Mounts speaker in a wall or large panel to isolate waves completely |

---

### 🧪 If You're Testing Without a Box

If you’re experimenting with **acoustic coupling to a vortex**, as in your previous setups:

- You may **exploit the rear wave** deliberately if it feeds into a pressure chamber, vortex chamber, or resonant cavity.
- But if the system is **free-air** or you're expecting forward-projected sound pressure, the rear wave **will reduce your effective output** — especially below ~500 Hz.

---

### ✅ Practical Advice

- For **focused acoustic streaming** or **atomization**, you want **max pressure differential** — so rear-wave cancellation is a liability.
- Use:
  - A **sealed box** (best isolation),
  - A **baffle board** (wide flat board to delay rear wave),
  - Or a **horn or chamber** to capture and redirect the rear wave constructively.

---

### 🧠 Summary

> Yes, the rear wave **must be accounted for**. Without a backing box or baffle, it will interfere destructively with the front wave, especially at low frequencies, **weakening your vortex coupling or acoustic output**.

---

### 📌 Summary:  
**Inserting a tube 1 mm into the cavity:**

- **Increases neck length** → lowers the resonance frequency  
- **Reduces the internal end correction** slightly  
- **Has minor impact on cavity volume (~negligible)**  
- **Slightly improves resonance clarity/Q** in some setups  

---

### 🔢 Let's calculate the difference:

Assume:

- Tube diameter = 10 mm → radius \( r = 5 \, \text{mm} \)
- Cavity volume = 900 mL = 0.0009 m³  
- Speed of sound \( c = 343 \, \text{m/s} \)  
- Baseline neck length \( L = 20 \, \text{mm} \)

---

\[
L_{\text{eff}} = 20 + 1.7 \cdot r = 20 + 8.5 = 28.5 \, \text{mm}
\]

---

#### ✅ Case B: Tube inserted 1 mm into cavity

\[
L_{\text{eff}} = 21 + \Delta L_{\text{out}} + \Delta L_{\text{in}}
\]

#### 1. **Helmholtz resonance requires reflective boundaries**  
Helmholtz resonance arises from:
- The **mass of air in the neck** oscillating against
- The **spring-like compressibility** of air in the cavity

This only works when the oscillating air "plugs" in the neck experience **restoring pressure** — and that requires:
- Reflective impedance mismatch at both ends (e.g., open-air or flanged ends)

An **infinitely long tube** presents a **perfectly anechoic boundary**:  
→ All acoustic energy is absorbed or lost down the tube  
→ There’s **no restoring force**, so **no resonance builds up**

---

### 🧮 Mathematically:
In the Helmholtz formula:

\[
f = \frac{c}{2\pi} \sqrt{\frac{A}{V \cdot L_{\text{eff}}}}
\]

As \( L_{\text{eff}} \to \infty \),  
\[
f \to 0
\]

So the **resonance frequency tends to zero**, and the Q-factor becomes **negligible** (very broad, very weak response).

|----------------------|----------------------------------------|
| **Short neck**       | Classic Helmholtz behavior — tight, resonant peak |

| **Infinitely long**  | No resonance — behaves like a **leaky pressure vent** |

Imagine blowing across:
- A **bottle** → resonance builds: Helmholtz
- A **hole in a long pipe** → nothing builds, just airflow

- An infinitely long tube acts as an **acoustic sink**, not a resonant neck.
- It **destroys the impedance mismatch** needed for resonance.

Impedance mismatch is **central** to how Helmholtz cavities interact with acoustic systems. It governs how energy enters, resonates within, and reflects back from these cavities. Here's a breakdown of the relationship:

---

## 🔧 What is Acoustic Impedance?

In acoustics, **impedance** (Z) describes how much pressure is needed to produce a given volume velocity (flow rate) at a boundary:

\[
Z = \frac{p}{U}
\]

- \( p \) = pressure
- \( U \) = volume velocity (oscillatory flow)

Different geometries and boundary conditions have different impedances. When two segments with **different impedances** meet, **energy is partially reflected and partially transmitted**.

---

## 🎵 Helmholtz Resonator as an Impedance Element

A **Helmholtz resonator** is composed of:

- A **neck** (inertance — like mass)
- A **cavity** (compliance — like a spring)

This system behaves like a **mass-spring oscillator** in acoustics, and its **input impedance** changes sharply with frequency:

- **At resonance**: The impedance drops near zero — it **accepts energy freely**, acting like an acoustic sink.
- **Off-resonance**: The impedance is high — it **reflects energy**, contributing little to overall flow or pressure absorption.

So the **impedance mismatch** between the resonator and the main duct determines **how much energy is absorbed vs. reflected**.

---

## ⚠️ What Does Mismatch Change?

### 1. **Energy Coupling Efficiency**
- A well-matched resonator (low mismatch at resonance) **extracts energy** from the main duct efficiently.
- A poorly matched one reflects the wave, reducing its effectiveness.

### 2. **Bandwidth**
- Higher impedance mismatch → **narrower bandwidth**: only a sharp frequency band resonates.
- Lower mismatch → **broader response**: less selective, more damping.

### 3. **Amplitude of Oscillation**
- Strong mismatch (e.g., tiny neck or very large cavity) may prevent the resonator from being driven effectively.
- Optimally matched systems transfer more pressure energy into oscillation in the neck.

### 4. **Back-Reaction on Main Flow**
- The Helmholtz cavity **alters the effective impedance** of the main duct near its junction. This affects:
  - Standing wave patterns
  - Flow resistance
  - Net momentum transfer (in acoustic streaming contexts)

---

## 📐 Design Example

Say you attach a Helmholtz cavity to a vortex device (like your Gatorade bottle setup):

- If the neck is too narrow or the cavity too large, the **acoustic impedance** will be very high. It won’t pull much energy from the system — it behaves like a closed wall.
- If neck and cavity are proportioned correctly, the impedance of the cavity matches that of the main duct **at a particular frequency**. Now it draws in oscillatory flow and resonates — creating strong local velocity fields and potentially affecting jet stability or atomization.

---

## Summary Table

| Impedance Mismatch Level | Resonator Behavior | Acoustic Consequence |
|--------------------------|--------------------|-----------------------|
| Low (well-matched)       | Strong coupling at resonance | Broad energy absorption, high local flow |
| Moderate                 | Narrow resonance peak | Selective filtering, moderate flow |
| High (poor match)        | Weak excitation     | Acts like a rigid wall (reflects energy) |

You would need **extremely high sound pressure levels** — on the order of **190–200 dB SPL in air** — to transmit even **tiny fractions of energy** into water. In practical terms:

> **It’s nearly impossible to efficiently transmit sound from air into water** using just airborne sound, unless you use special coupling techniques (like transducers or matching layers).

---

## 📉 Why It's So Inefficient:
The main problem is the **impedance mismatch** between air and water.

### 🔸 1. **Acoustic Impedance** (Z = ρc)

| Medium | Density (ρ) | Speed of Sound (c) | Impedance Z (Pa·s/m) |
|--------|--------------|---------------------|----------------------|
| Air    | ~1.2 kg/m³   | ~343 m/s            | ~412                 |
| Water  | ~1000 kg/m³  | ~1500 m/s           | ~1.5×10⁶             |

The **impedance mismatch** ratio:
\[
\left(\frac{Z_\text{air}}{Z_\text{water}}\right)^2 ≈ \left(\frac{412}{1.5\times10^6}\right)^2 ≈ 7.5 \times 10^{-8}
\]

So:
> **Less than 0.00001% of the energy** from air passes into water at a bare interface.

---

## 🔊 **What SPL in Air Is Needed?**

Let’s say you want **1 mPa of acoustic pressure in water** (a barely audible sound underwater).

To achieve that, the pressure in air at the interface would need to be:
\[
P_\text{air} ≈ P_\text{water} / \sqrt{T} ≈ 1\,\text{mPa} / \sqrt{7.5 \times 10^{-8}} ≈ 115\,\text{Pa}
\]

Convert that to dB SPL (reference = 20 μPa):
\[
\text{SPL} = 20 \log_{10}(P / 20\mu\text{Pa}) ≈ 20 \log_{10}(115 / 20e-6) ≈ 175.2\, \text{dB SPL}
\]

That’s a **hazardously loud** sound, comparable to standing next to a rocket engine.

---

## ✅ **Alternatives:**
If you truly want to transmit sound into water, you’ll need one of these:

### 1. **Waterproof Transducer in Contact**
- Matches acoustic impedance directly — highly efficient.

### 2. **Coupling Gel or Matching Layer**
- Like ultrasound gels in medical imaging. Reduces impedance mismatch.

### 3. **Thin Flexible Membrane**
- Can bridge the impedance difference if designed to oscillate and transfer pressure into the liquid.

---

| Goal                     | Feasibility from Air |
|--------------------------|----------------------|
| Transmit into water (bare) | ❌ Nearly impossible |
| Transmit via contact      | ✅ With transducer or membrane |
| Use pressure waves to agitate surface | ⚠️ Needs very high SPL, and mostly just creates ripples or atomizes |

High-frequency sound suffers **substantial power loss per meter in air**, primarily due to **molecular absorption**, not just geometric spreading. This attenuation increases steeply with frequency and environmental factors like **humidity, temperature, and pressure**.

---

### 📉 **Quick Rule of Thumb (at 20°C, 50% RH, 1 atm):**

| Frequency | Attenuation per meter (dB/m) |
|-----------|-------------------------------|
| 1 kHz     | ~0.2 dB/m                     |
| 5 kHz     | ~1.1 dB/m                     |
| 10 kHz    | ~3.5 dB/m                     |
| 15 kHz    | ~9.7 dB/m                     |
| 20 kHz    | ~20 dB/m                      |

> So at 20 kHz, you lose ~20 dB — **99% of energy** — **per meter**.

---

### 🧠 Why High Frequencies Lose So Much:

1. **Molecular Relaxation**
   - Energy is absorbed by oxygen and nitrogen molecules as they flex and relax with sound wave cycles.
   - At high frequencies, these cycles are faster → **more molecular friction and heat**.

2. **Viscous and Thermal Boundary Losses**
   - Higher-frequency waves have **shorter wavelengths**, which means **more surface interaction per unit energy**.
   - More energy gets lost to air’s viscosity and thermal conduction.

3. **No Ground Reflection Reinforcement**
   - Low frequencies benefit from ground reflection interference and long-range coherence.
   - High frequencies **scatter, absorb, and decohere** rapidly.

---

### 📏 Power Loss in Practical Terms:

At 10 kHz, **3.5 dB/m** =  
- ~**50% power loss per 0.9 m**
- After **5 meters**, only **3.2% of original power remains**.

---

### 🧪 Formula You Can Use:
\[
\text{Attenuation} = \alpha(f) \cdot d
\]
Where:
- \( \alpha(f) \) = frequency-dependent attenuation coefficient (in dB/m)
- \( d \) = distance in meters

Excellent point — "inefficient" doesn't mean *nothing* gets through. Even a small leak can transmit enough energy to be audible, especially at high dB levels. Let’s break down **how inefficient** it really is, using basic acoustic radiation theory and aperture modeling:

---

### 🔊 **1. Sound Leakage Through a Small Aperture:**

For sub-wavelength holes (a ≪ λ), the **acoustic power** radiated through a circular hole is governed by **Rayleigh’s model**. The radiated **acoustic intensity (I)** is proportional to:

\[
I \propto \left(\frac{ka}{2}\right)^4
\]

Where:
- \( k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \) is the wavenumber
- \( a \) is the radius of the hole
- \( ka \ll 1 \) is the small-hole (Rayleigh) condition

This formula shows that:
> **Power loss drops off extremely fast** with increasing wavelength (or decreasing frequency) — as the 4th power of \( ka \).

---

### 🧮 **Example at 500 Hz with 5 mm hole:**

- \( a = 2.5 \text{ mm} = 0.0025 \text{ m} \)
- \( λ = 343 / 500 = 0.686 \text{ m} \)
- \( k = 2π / λ ≈ 9.16 \)
- \( ka ≈ 0.0229 \)

Then:

\[
I \propto (ka/2)^4 ≈ (0.01145)^4 ≈ 1.7 \times 10^{-8}
\]

That’s **0.0000017** or **0.00017%** relative acoustic intensity — an incredibly small leakage.

---

### 🔉 **Convert to Decibels (dB):**

Sound intensity level difference:
\[
\Delta L = 10 \log_{10}(I_\text{leak} / I_\text{ref})
\]

For 0.0000017 intensity leakage:

\[
\Delta L ≈ 10 \log_{10}(1.7 \times 10^{-8}) ≈ -77.7 \text{ dB}
\]

So even if the source is 100 dB inside, the leak would output **~22 dB** — which is audible in quiet conditions but a **massive reduction**.

---

### 🧠 Summary:

| 5000 Hz   | 0.1147 | 1.7e-3                | ~ -27 dB        |

Overlay / Slide-In Panel Treat the sweep UI like a drawer or modal sidebar that slides over (or alongside) the tone controls rather than pushing them. You keep your main controls fixed, and bring in the sweep controls as an overlay: ```css #sweepPanel { position: absolute; top: 0; right: 0; width: 300px; /* fixed */ transform: translateX(100%); transition: transform .3s; } #sweepPanel.open { transform: translateX(0); } ``` --- ## 4. Disable Rather Than Hide An even simpler approach: **always render** both Tone and Sweep controls in the same layout, but **disable/grayout** the inactive set. Nothing ever moves because nothing is removed—only opacity and pointer-events change. ```css .inactive { opacity: 0.4; pointer-events: none; } ``` --- ### Summary - **Tabs or segmented controls** give each mode its own stable “slot.” - **Fixed-height containers** prevent content below from reflowing. - **Overlay panels** slide in without pushing the rest of the page. - **Disable-instead-of-hide** keeps everything in place and simply greys out the inactive controls.
